cells.tense: You are at the bench now, and the work deepens with each pass.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Find one place in the work where two things have gone blurry together. Spend twenty minutes cutting them apart until you can say plainly why they differ. One edge, not a whole session.
cells.core:
The building is going well and you can feel it. Each pass adds what the last one didn't, and the repetition isn't dull, because the difference between a pass that holds and one that doesn't is getting clearer to you. That clarity is the engine. It also happens where nobody's watching — you're alone with it most of the time, and the being alone feeds the work instead of starving you.

The refinement is running clean, which means it hasn't turned into checking. To keep it that way, take the one edge that's gone blurry — where two things have quietly merged — and cut them apart until you can say why they differ. Twenty minutes on that edge, once this week. Keeps the eye careful without making the checking a second job.

cells.verb: Build a craft deeper with each pass

cells.tense: You will have it finished in your head by then, and the bench will still be waiting.
cells.act: mark the good thing together, out loud
cells.ask: Tell someone about one piece that's done as it stands — out loud, the finished thing and not the plan. Then stay in the conversation instead of shrinking what you said.
cells.core:
You're braced against a version of this that doesn't exist yet. The finished piece is already built in your head, so the actual passes — slow, half-formed — read as behind schedule against it. You push to close a gap that only exists in the future tense, and the endurance that used to be holding is turning into bracing.

What this needs is the other people who'd know what it cost. Tell someone about one finished piece, out loud, exactly as it stands — not the plan, and not with the rough parts edited out first. Let the gladness go into the room and stay there. That's what the work is for, not a break from it. Marking it with someone takes the pressure down to the size of the actual job.

cells.tense: You stood at the door a long time, and it is behind you now.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Write the shape of the work on one page — what it is, what it isn't, the order things happen in — and set it where someone else will come across it before they ask. Write it once and stop adding to it.
cells.core:
The building stopped and the endurance that used to carry it is holding nothing. You show up in the place where the work was, and the work isn't there with you. Nobody has said anything, and nobody has to — that's how it stands, not a verdict on it.

What's starved isn't effort, it's the frame. Put the shape of the work on one page: what it is, what it isn't, the order things happen in. Set that page where someone else will come across it before they ask. Not a pitch — the shape, stated once, plain. Reading it in someone else's hands tells you whether there's a there there. If the page comes up empty, that's an answer too, and you can do something with it.
cells.sheetLine: You stand where the work was, and it isn't with you.

cells.tense: You are keeping all of it steady and calling it just how you are.
cells.act: move at the pace your feeling can sustain
cells.ask: Take a long stretch of the work at a tempo you could hold past the end of it, not the tempo of a single day. Stay at that pace through the stretch, then notice what pulled toward faster.
cells.core:
There's a steady hand on this whole thing, and you'd describe it as just keeping it together. Kept, though, is what it is — the frame hasn't cracked, and that's something you're doing, not something that happened to you. What's unowned isn't the effort. It's that you set the pace. Somewhere you decided how fast this moves, and you've been living inside that decision without calling it a decision.

So take a long stretch at a tempo you could hold past the end of it, not the tempo of a single day, and keep to that pace through the stretch. Then notice what pulled toward faster. That pull is information — it tells you whose schedule you've been keeping. Choose the tempo your own feeling can carry, and the keeping stops being something you do to yourself.
